On their own , the microplastics ingested by a species may not pose a significant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stress due to rising sea temperatures , the consequences can be different . " These combined effects , they can be cumulative in the organism , " Catarino explained . <h> Methods to identify microplastics <p> Marine microplastics are difficult to identify and quantify due to their small dimensions , irregular shape , and , sometimes , different colours . <p> Despite these challenges , recognising microplastics is possible , and VLIZ 's postdoctoral researcher Nelle Meyers has worked on a semi-automated method to identify them . <p> This technique involves collecting a sample from the sea using a net , cleaning the sample of organic materials , and staining it with Nile Red before placing it under a microscope . A fluorescence colouration analysis is then run and its results are passed through two automated programmes that can identify whether a particle is a microplastic or not and what type of microplastic it is . <p> " We wanted to automate to speed up the whole process , " Meyers said . " We wrote a code so when you upload the picture , the image analysis is done @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ semi-automated step and the use of a fluorescence microscope , which is relatively common in laboratories , Meyers claimed the technique is cost- and time-effective . <p> However , the method also presents some limitations , as it lacks information about the chemical composition of the particles and can determine only certain types of polymers . <h> Microplastics ' impact on marine species <p> Just as larger plastic debris is ingested by marine species , tiny plastic particles can also be consumed by smaller organisms , like plankton . <p> " They microplastics can also get their stomach , their gut clogged . And then they small organisms do n't eat their nutrients , they do n't eat their own food , " Catarino explained . <p> " And this is worrying because then it brings other issues because these organisms are not able to reproduce and their population will not strive , so it will be affected , " she said . <p> The specific effects of microplastics depend on multiple factors , including the marine species involved , the type of microplastics , and other stressors to which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ temperature , ocean acidification , and more . <p> " Sometimes it 's not just one issue or another , it 's the accumulation of all these effects that may be harmful to the organisms , " Catarino told Euronews Next .

@@139284242 <h> Huey Perry : A climate disaster nears , but who among us cares ? <p> Suppose NASA interrupted every television station in America with an emergency announcement that a 10-mile-wide asteroid had been detected and that every calculation showed it would collide with Earth in 30 years . There would be no debate over whether it was real . The president would immediately assemble the world 's brightest scientists and engineers . Congress would appropriate whatever money was required . Every nation with the ability to help would join the effort . Television networks would interrupt their regular programming with constant updates . Every scientific breakthrough would become front-page news . The objective would be simple : do whatever is necessary to change the asteroid 's course . Virtually no one would object because everyone would understand that the survival of civilization depended upon it . <p> Now consider another warning . One of our leading universities -- the Massachusetts Institute of Technology -- recently concluded that unless humanity takes corrective action , large portions of our planet could become uninhabitable within the next 30 years . Thousands of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , observations and increasingly sophisticated computer models . Yet instead of uniting behind the science , we have divided ourselves . Millions accept the warnings while millions of others dismiss them . Some insist immediate action is essential , while others argue there is no crisis at all . The evidence continues to accumulate , but public opinion remains sharply divided . <p> Perhaps the difference is not in the science but in the way the human mind responds to danger . An asteroid is dramatic . We can picture it racing toward Earth , and we understand instantly what the outcome will be if nothing is done . Climate change arrives differently . It advances one heat wave , one flood , one wildfire , one drought , and one failed harvest at a time . Because each event occurs separately , we tend to see them as isolated incidents rather than as pieces of a much larger pattern . Gradually we become accustomed to what only a few years earlier would have seemed unimaginable . <p> Nature , however , is indifferent to our opinions . The atmosphere @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or public opinion polls . It responds only to the laws of physics . While we continue debating , greenhouse gases continue to accumulate , oceans continue to warm , glaciers continue to melt , and weather patterns continue to change . The planet simply keeps moving in the direction that science says it will unless that course is altered . <p> One thought continues to trouble me . Humanity has always demonstrated an extraordinary ability to solve problems once everyone accepts that the danger is real . We have landed on the moon , eradicated diseases , split the atom , mapped the human genome , and placed spacecraft beyond our solar system . We have remarkable intelligence and unlimited creativity when we choose to use them . The question is whether we will recognize the danger before the opportunity to lessen its consequences slips beyond our reach . <p> If an asteroid were heading toward Earth , the world would unite almost overnight . The mystery is why we can recognize one threat so clearly while remaining uncertain about another that unfolds before our eyes every single day @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ happening now . Just last week Canada was on fire , heat domes spread over Europe and on and on . You know before I forget it , it 's been pretty hot here .

@@139306147 <p> The next in the monthly series by WWF-India that highlights niche and unconventional green careers through the stories of well-known personalities from the field of environment and conservation <p> Nearly 30 years ago , I received an unexpected phone call late one night . There is a difference , however , between the default belief that certain predictions are wrong and the default belief that certain predictions are embarrassing . As recently as the nineteen-nineties , when Wired magazine seemed like a monthly dispatch from beyond the event horizon , the fashionable pose to assume was one of electric optimism . Now it is distinctly unfashionable to get overly worked up one way or another about technological novelty . The adoption of an inductive argument about the future -- one in which the sun always rises because the sun has always risen -- has come to function as a marker of temperament . We are the sort of people who can see through the hysteria and the hype ; you are the sort of people who consider yourselves specially elected to witness the singularity . @@139338449 <p> The 2024/25 rainy season will be remembered in history books as one of the hardest Israel has ever known . For the average hiker , the drought is a matter of a yellower landscape or a lower Sea of Galilee , but for the ecosystems of the northern part of the country , it is not that simple . Dr. Asaf Tsoar , head of the Environment Division at the Nature and Parks Authority , reveals a troubling truth : Natural drought is only the first stage in the story . " The real enemy of the streams is not the closed skies , but human management and water allocation that leaves nature as the last consumer in line , " Dr. Tsoar explains in a new study published on Sunday in the journal Man and Nature -- A Journal for Nature Conservation in Israel . <h> The numbers behind the drought <p> The meteorological data from the past year leave no room for doubt . In the Sea of Galilee drainage basin , only 40% to 45% of the average rainfall fell . The impact on the sources @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Dan Stream , one of the main lifelines of the North , plummeted last December to an all-time low of 1.8 cubic meters per second . " To understand the magnitude of the catastrophe , one must remember that the multi-year average for this month stood until today at 5.9 cubic meters per second , " Dr. Tsoar says . <p> Although local nature is accustomed to dry years , the combination of extreme drought and artificial water extraction for drinking and agriculture created an emergency in aquatic habitats . " The problem begins when artificial extraction joins the natural drought . For the streams , springs , and marshes , the question is not only how much rain fell , but how much water remained in them after man finished pumping , diverting , and allocating the precious resource , " Dr. Tsoar says . <p> ' ' The real enemy of the streams is not the closed skies , but human management and water allocation . ' ' Hermon Stream ( Banias ) ( credit : OFER SHINAR/NATURE AND PARKS AUTHORITY ) <h> The river 's death spiral @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the ecosystem begins to unravel . First , the water level drops , and the vital connection between the flow and bank vegetation is severed . Later , rocks are exposed and the surface area available to animals decreases significantly . Shallow flow habitats on a stony substrate disappear , and in their place , standing pools are formed that could become a death trap for certain species . <p> The damage is not only visual but also chemical : In standing pools , water quality rapidly declines . The concentration of dissolved substances rises , temperatures surge , and oxygen concentrations -- essential for life -- plummet . In such a situation , the dilution capacity for pollutants is zero , and algae develop in abnormal quantities . At the end of the process , the continuity of the stream is broken and parts of it dry up completely , leading to irreversible damage to biodiversity . <h> The Battle for Hapkak Bridge <p> One of the main points of friction occurred this year in the Jordan River , at Hapkak Bridge measurement point . Even though only @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Galilee basin , the Water Authority proposed reducing even further the minimum flow rates set for the stream . The Nature and Parks Authority , the Environmental Protection Ministry , and the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel strongly opposed the move , as the proposed reduction was greater than a third of the threshold that had already been defined as the absolute minimum for a drought year . " The debate is not just over abstract values of nature , " Dr. Tsoar says . " A weak flow in the Jordan raises direct risks to public health and the economy . In the opposition documents , it was clarified that a drastic drop in flow rate could lead to the closure of stream sections to hikers due to pollution , which would critically harm tourism and recreational activities that constitute an economic anchor for the entire region . Water for nature is not a luxury ; it is a basic condition for a functioning regional system . " Ultimately , the Water Council agreed to amend the quantity , although to a lesser extent than demanded @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : From statement to reality <p> The principle of the " nature 's right to water " is not new in Israel : As early as 2000 , a government decision was adopted allocating 50 million cubic meters per year for the restoration of stream flows . In 2004 , the Water Law was even amended , defining nature as one of the official entities entitled to the use of water . The legal significance is that nature is not supposed to suffice with only the " leftovers " of other consumers , but is a legitimate consumer with defined needs . However , the reality on the ground , especially in dry years , shows that the law does not always pass the test of reality . The main lesson from the recent drought is that preparation must begin long before the flow meter shows zero . Responsible water management in an era of climate change requires a shift from " firefighting " to long-term planning and preparing the system for periods of water scarcity , something the Water Authority is leading together with partners such as water associations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rivers <p> To prevent the next drying of streams , the Nature and Parks Authority together with the Water Authority are building a strategic plan based on arriving early at the discussion table with solid data . The plan includes : <p> Setting minimum thresholds : Creating thresholds that can not be changed even in moments of pressure . Infrastructure and alternatives : Building supply alternatives for agriculture , including smart winter impoundment and connection to regional supply systems , so they do not have to rely on stream water in dry years . Enforcement mechanisms : Fighting illegal water captures and freeing springs for nature where possible . Science-based monitoring : Decision-making based on field measurements rather than momentary political pressures . <p> Despite the difficult picture , there is room for cautious optimism . " Experience shows that when water returns and its quality improves , wet habitats know how to respond and recover quickly . However , this recovery does not grant a ' license to gamble ' on the future of the stream . If we continue to treat streams as a leftover , we will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . " The real test will be in building a true partnership with water managers , which will ensure that even in the hardest years , ' the tap ' will not be closed completely on Israeli nature . @@139391546 <h> The world 's rainiest towns are running short of something to drink . In Meghalaya , the crisis is not about how much rain falls , but about who captures it , who stores it , and who is left to pay for it <p> By November , the streams around Sohra begin to fall silent . The rivers that roared through the monsoon thin to a trickle and then to nothing , and the springs that families have drawn from for generations turn seasonal . By deep winter , in a town that holds two world records for rainfall , people are buying water by the bucket . <p> A bucket carted up from the plains costs anywhere between ? 20 and ? 50 , depending on the month . Some households pay close to a thousand rupees for 500 litres . The residents of Sohra , the town the world still calls Cherrapunji , describe the shortage plainly : from November to March , water is something you purchase . What was once perennial is now seasonal . What was once shared is now sold . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Sohra and neighbouring Mawsynram are among the wettest inhabited places on earth , drenched by an average of over 11,000 mm of rainfall a year -- figures that dwarf almost anywhere else on the planet . Yet in the winter dry months , at least 40% of residents in the Sohra constituency face an acute shortage of potable water , buying it from private contractors at prices that rise with scarcity . Ahead of successive Assembly elections , drinking water has become a campaign promise made to more than 25,000 voters , and broken with equal regularity . <p> The paradox of Meghalaya is not that the rain has stopped . It is that abundance has never guaranteed access -- and that the State built almost nothing to hold on to what the sky gives it . <h> The rain is changing <p> The first pressure is the rain itself . The monsoon that once blotted out the sun for months now arrives in shorter , sharper bursts . Older residents remember a childhood when the rain was so relentless that a clear sky was a novelty ; today , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The trend is measurable . A study by researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology , Kharagpur , and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology , Pune -- drawing on rain-gauge records across Northeast India from 1901 to 2019 -- found a clear long-term decline in rainfall across the region . Sohra has been losing an estimated 27.15 mm of rainfall a year over roughly the past four decades . The slide has already cost the town its title as the wettest place on earth , a distinction that has passed to Mawsynram , barely 15 km away . Even Mawsynram is now recording a decrease . <p> The researchers trace the reduction in part to rising sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea , which are altering the moisture carried inland during the crucial pre-monsoon window . Satellite records point to a second , more local driver : the loss of vegetation cover across the Northeast over the past two decades . As forests give way to croplands , both the rainfall and the land 's ability to absorb it decline together . <h> Rain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ problem is geology and slope . Sohra sits atop a high limestone plateau , and rain that falls on it drains away almost at once , sheeting down the hillsides and eventually reaching the plains of Bangladesh far below . Very little is retained on the way down . Deforestation has stripped the soil of what capacity it had to hold water , so that the rain the town does receive rolls off the hills largely unharvested . <p> This is the heart of the matter . The defining question in Meghalaya is no longer how much rain falls , but how little of it is captured , stored and managed . The State was configured , over centuries , around the assumption of endless water -- its economy , its agriculture , its settlements . It was never built to keep water for a dry season , because a dry season was never supposed to come . Unlike arid regions that invest heavily in storage precisely because they expect scarcity , Meghalaya 's steep terrain means that when the rain fails , water simply runs off and the hillsides @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when the State recorded a rainfall deficit of about 80% in June -- normally the peak of the monsoon -- under the influence of El Ni ? o . Chief Minister Conrad K. Sangma called it an " existential crisis " and warned officials that climate change was " no longer a future challenge " but a " present reality " . For a State whose entire socio-economic fabric is built on water , a shortfall of that scale in a single monsoon month is genuinely destabilising . The Mawphlang dam , a key reservoir supplying drinking water to the capital Shillong , has been reported drying up during such spells -- its catchment further degraded by stone quarrying . <h> Who carries the buckets ? <p> A water crisis is never distributed evenly , and Meghalaya 's is no exception . In many localities , water trickles from communal taps for only a short window each day . Those who miss it walk several kilometres to natural springs , a burden that falls overwhelmingly on women and children , who spend a large part of the day hauling buckets @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ who can afford to , buy from private contractors ; those who can not , walk . <p> The State 's formal water infrastructure has not filled the gap . Under the Jal Jeevan Mission , launched in 2019 to bring a functional tap connection to every rural household , Meghalaya has lagged the rest of the country -- rural tap-water coverage stood at around 43.57% in 2023 , against a national average of roughly 55.32% . In the Garo Hills , reports have described taps installed with no water behind them , and taps left unconnected to any pipe at all . The shortfall reaches into schools : of roughly 14,600 schools in the State , only about 6,720 were recorded as having functional drinking water -- a gap that grows more serious as climate-driven heatwaves raise the risk of dehydration among children . <h> A crisis of management , not just weather <p> It would be easy to file Meghalaya 's predicament under climate change and leave it there . The declining rainfall is real , and the fingerprints of a warming Indian Ocean are on it . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as much about governance as about weather . Rain that runs off unharvested , catchments degraded by quarrying , tap schemes that exist only on paper , and a decade of election promises that dissolve after polling day -- none of these are meteorological failures . <p> The State 's own institutions have begun to acknowledge this . The Meghalaya Water Foundation has argued that people , as the users of water , must be placed at the centre of any solution rather than treated as passive recipients of pipes . The draft Integrated State Water Policy , prepared by the Department of Water Resources , is built around sustainable management and community participation -- and if it delivers , it could offer a template for other water-stressed States and cities from Chennai to Bengaluru now confronting their own contradictions of flood and drought . <p> The practical priorities are not mysterious : harvest the rain that currently runs to Bangladesh , protect and reforest critical catchments such as Mawphlang , rein in quarrying and unplanned land-use change , and invest in the storage and distribution that the State never @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ political follow-through . <p> The rain still falls on Meghalaya 's hills , if less reliably than before . The failure lies in how little of it reaches the people who live beneath them . If the wettest place on earth can leave its residents queuing for water , the lesson for the rest of India -- where water is far scarcer -- is difficult to ignore . <p> Adarsh Ashok is a public policy professional working in government advisory . @@139404656 <h> This Is The First Satellite Constellation Made To Detect Wildfires Before They Grow <p> There is very little doubt that global warming and climate change are increasing the number , size , and intensity of wildfires across the globe . Indeed , according to NASA research , both the northern and western forests of North America are among the areas hardest hit by the rise in extreme wildfires . The wildfire " season " also seems to be getting longer , too . For instance , in the Western U.S. , the fire season is now more than a month longer than it was 35 years ago . <p> As wildfires continue to spread at increasing rates , scientists have needed to develop more sophisticated technology to detect them . One such technology involves using a satellite constellation called FireSat to spot wildfires early . Launched on July 7 , 2026 aboard SpaceX 's Transporter 17 Mission , the FireSat constellation currently has three active satellites . The system has already been tested with the launch of a prototype satellite known as " Protoflight , " which spent a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It successfully detected wildfires and even detected a small roadside fire in Oregon that other systems had missed . <p> The project is led by Muon Space , which is working with various partners to get the system operational . The non-profit Earth Fire Alliance ( EFA ) is one of the main stakeholders , with additional support coming from Bezos Earth Fund , the Betty Moore Foundation , and Google , among others . While this is certainly a more expensive option than the student-built drone designed to help solve America 's wildfire problem , the team behind it hopes it can save more than $1 billion annually in fire damages in the U.S. alone . <h> How the FireSat satellites work <p> The first three operational satellites are built on the Condor-M satellite . Modular spacecraft designed specifically for low-Earth orbit , the FireSat satellites are fitted out with a multispectral infrared imaging system that captures six different bands of infrared light . The wide spectral range allows the satellites to detect fires as small as about 16 square feet , even through cloud or smoke cover @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ detect fires at lower temperatures . Impressively , each spacecraft covers a swath of land roughly 930 miles per pass . <p> The Muon Halo platform on which the constellation is based provides the technology required for FireSat 's real-time processing . It probably is n't a surprise to find out that AI is also being used . With contributions from Google , AI is used to help the system process the information in nearly real-time . The system works by comparing the current photo with thousands of others from the same spot . AI takes into account the weather and various other factors before determining if a " thermal anomaly " is actually fire . <p> With the current trio of satellites , the system can image fire-prone locations on Earth roughly twice a day . However , by the time the full 50 planned satellites are launched , it 's hoped that each location on Earth will be imaged once every 20 minutes , with vulnerable areas imaged more frequently . The next step for EFA and Muon Space is to be able to image vulnerable areas hourly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Images <p> The last few decades have seen wildfires become faster , hotter , and more destructive . Droughts and rising temperatures are adding the " fuel " needed for such fires to proliferate , with higher nighttime temperatures also important as cooler nights used to help slow the progress of fires . While wildfires are a natural phenomenon , human activity is behind many of them , with one of the leading causes of wildfires sitting in your driveway ( your car ) . <p> According to the National Interagency Fire Center , there have been 41,984 fires across the U.S. between January 1 , 2026 and July 24 , 2026 , affecting over 4 million acres . For comparison , there were 39,279 fires recorded , affecting just shy of 3 million acres , in the same period in 2025 . In fact , wildfires account for around half of all annual tree losses across the globe . In addition to the risk that fires pose to civilians , firefighting personnel , and property , research shows that smoke from wildfires is also resulting in poor air quality @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This is why FireSat is so important . Its ability to spot even small fires and report them to the relevant authorities in near real-time could greatly reduce how many of these fires become uncontrollable . While FireSat satellites may not yet be considered among the most important satellite launches in history , they certainly have the potential to save lives , property , and wildlife . 
@@139407740 <h> Tropical Diseases Like Dengue Fever and Chikungunya Are on the Rise in Europe <p> Climate change is helping invasive species to not only establish themselves across the continent but to stay alive for longer . Scientists suggest we get used to it . <p> Photo-Illustration : Jobanny Cabrera ; Getty Images <p> In September 2024 , a handful of patients showed up at the emergency room in the coastal city of Fano , Italy , with mysterious symptoms : a rash on their hands and feet , fever , nausea , and diarrhea . Doctors sent for various tests until one came back with a positive result for dengue , a viral infection spread by mosquitoes , usually in tropical regions of the world . They tested the other patients , and , sure enough , they had dengue too . The strange thing ? None of the patients had recently traveled to a country where they might expect to pick up a dengue infection . The only thing they had in common was visiting a particular neighbourhood in Fano . <p> As climate change increases temperatures across Europe @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Europeans would usually think about only when traveling to other continents . The Fano outbreak was n't the first time dengue had been detected as spreading locally in mainland Europe , but it was significantly larger than previous incidents , with 199 cases detected between mid-August and mid-October of 2024 . Over the past few years , European countries have reported outbreaks of other mosquito-borne viruses such as chikungunya , a painful disease that causes joint swelling , and West Nile virus . In a heating world , so-called tropical diseases are no longer restricted to tropical regions -- and researchers expect the trend to continue . <p> The main current culprit is the mosquito Aedes albopictus , commonly known as the Asian tiger mosquito ( or just the tiger mosquito , given it 's now found across all continents ) . Unlike many mosquito species , it bites in the daytime as well as at night . The tiger mosquito already has established populations across Europe , particularly in the south , and we can expect it to move north , says Riccardo Moretti , a senior researcher at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Sustainable Economic Development ( ENEA ) , who has been working on tiger mosquitos for more than 20 years . <p> The tiger mosquito thrives between 20 and 30 degrees Celsius ( 68 to 86 Fahrenheit ) , but it can still live at around 10 Celsius ( 50 Fahrenheit ) . " This means that at the moment there are already conditions that could allow for the spread of the Asian tiger mosquito , even in England , " Moretti says . At the moment , these conditions are limited to the warmest part of the year in northern European countries . But farther south , such as in Greece , the mosquito season is elongating . Moretti says researchers have found adults buzzing around until December and reappearing already in March ; they overwinter as eggs . " There is a concrete risk that in the next few years , we could have a population capable of surviving throughout the year , " Moretti says . <p> At the moment , cases of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe tend to occur toward the end of summer . This is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ also when more people return from travel . Someone unwittingly brings back an infection that is n't found in Europe -- dengue , say -- and gets bitten by a tiger mosquito . The mosquito goes on to bite other people , and the disease spreads locally . But as the weather cools , the mosquitoes get less active and cases subside . If the mosquito season lasts longer , however , more infections can occur . Ultimately , says Moretti , there 's a risk that tropical diseases like dengue could become endemic in parts of Europe , meaning the disease is always there . " It is completely different dealing with occasional cases of virus transmission , and instead dealing with a permanent status of possibility of transmission , " he says . <p> A difference of a couple of degrees can make a big difference . Earlier this year , a study found that the conditions required for tiger mosquitoes to transmit chikungunya were cooler than previously thought . The mosquitoes can spread the virus at just 14 degrees Celsius ( 57 degrees Fahrenheit ) rather than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ occur in most European countries and for longer periods . " That difference of two degrees matters a lot when we are talking about global warming , " says Sandeep Tegar , an epidemiological modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology , who led the study . <p> While warmer temperatures may generally create better conditions for mosquitoes , this is n't the full story . Too hot -- more than 35 degrees Celsius ( 95 degrees Fahrenheit ) -- and tiger mosquitoes struggle to survive . Southern France and Spain , impacted by recent heat waves and wildfires , may actually have fewer mosquitoes this year , says Frederic Bartumeus , an ecologist at the Spanish scientific research center CEAB : " It 's not been a great mosquito season in these areas , because it 's too hot and it 's too dry . " <p> Rain is important , as mosquitoes need standing water to breed : This is where they lay their eggs , and where the larvae and pupae develop . " If it rains too little , then there 's not sufficient @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? lez , technology lead and expert in climate and infectious diseases at the UK-based health foundation Wellcome . " But if it rains too much , then it can wash away the mosquito breeding sites . " Humidity also plays a role . Beyond mosquitoes , climate conditions can have different effects on the viruses they carry , and on the behavior of humans -- an important consideration in the spread of disease . This all makes modeling patterns of mosquitoes and the diseases they spread more complex , so ongoing surveillance is critical . <p> It may be possible to reduce mosquito populations if they 're caught early enough . ENEA 's Moretti is part of a team that recently ran an experiment to control a tiger mosquito population in Italy by releasing more than a million male mosquitoes that were reproductively incompatible -- meaning when they mate , the female lays sterile eggs . This significantly reduced the number of fertile mosquito eggs in the area . But breeding mosquitoes in a specialized biofactory was expensive . In this case , the mosquitoes were bred in Miami @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> In any case , it would be impossible to eliminate mosquitoes , Moretti says -- they 're too efficient at colonizing new areas . " But what is important is to drastically reduce the risks of transmissions of tropical viruses . " <p> Col ? n Gonz ? lez says the main test for European countries is whether public health systems can keep isolated outbreaks from becoming major crises . " A common misconception is that preparedness is mainly about predicting disease outbreaks , " he says . " In reality , preparedness is about building the system that allows the public health infrastructure to effectively react when the risks emerge . " In this regard , Europe has an advantage over some parts of the world : Reliable public health and information systems mean that , so far , cases of mosquito-transmitted diseases have remained lower than in other areas of the world with a similar climate . <p> As invasive mosquitoes continue to settle across the Continent , Europeans may have to get used to taking the kinds of precautions that people in tropical regions are accustomed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on his windows and regularly empties standing water , such as that left sitting in flower pots . He uses mosquito repellant and wears long trousers if he 's going to be outside in the evening . " Simple things like that , that 's the only thing you can do , " he says . <p> Soon , the tiger mosquito may have company . Another invasive species , Aedes aegypti , or the yellow fever mosquito , has already established populations in Cyprus and the Portuguese archipelago of Madeira . As its name would suggest , it can transmit yellow fever , but it also carries dengue , chikungunya , and Zika . Yellow fever mosquitoes ca n't tolerate temperatures quite as cool as the tiger mosquito can , but it has been detected making occasional jaunts north , likely transported on cargo . @@139407752 <h> How to Bring a Geothermal Well Back From the Dead <p> Energy startup Zanskar has created one of the most productive geothermal wells in the US at a power plant that had been in decline for years . <p> Courtesy of Zanskar <p> Geothermal company Zanskar bought a New Mexico power plant in 2024 that appeared from the outside to be failing . The shallow wells had been rapidly losing heat , and the plant was having trouble generating power as a result . <p> Now , after drilling a new well and operating the power plant for a full year , Zanskar says that it has made a complete turnaround . In theory , it 's an excellent way of generating renewable baseload power : People have been harnessing steam from hot springs for thousands of years . But geographic constraints -- power plants need to be situated on geothermal reserves , which are overwhelmingly in the western US -- as well as the difficulty and expense traditionally involved in finding new wells mean geothermal energy constitutes less than 1 percent of the electricity mix in the US . <p> Courtesy of Zanskar <p> Another challenge for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The onsite 15-megawatt power plant , which supplies electricity to New Mexico 's largest utility , was designed to operate at temperatures above 300 degrees F. <p> While conventional geothermal wells usually go down 3,000 to 5,000 feet , drilling deeper wells can tap into hotter reserves of water to use for power . The company used the technology last year to make a discovery in Nevada , and it says that same modeling also helped pinpoint where to most productively drill at the Lightning Dock site . It combined those models with drill bit technology refined by the oil and gas industry , which helped it drill deeper holes 35 percent faster at what Zanskar says is a " competitive cost . " ( The company did n't provide specifics . ) The new 8,000-foot well has been operating for a full year , with heat levels above where they were before the decline . <p> " We knew that if we were going to buy this field , we were committed to drilling deeper and going after it , " says Joel Edwards , a cofounder of Zanskar . Venture capital investors -- who typically have veered away from geothermal -- have also been putting money into the industry , says Stephanie Diaz , a senior associate at BloombergNEF . Because of this , companies like Fervo have been the focus of much of the recent investment and attention in the industry , Diaz says . <p> But Diaz says data-driven approaches like Zanskar 's can help de-risk traditional geothermal development . @@139407753 <h> NASA 's New 3D Model Shows the Earth Is a Lumpy Mess <p> We like to think of our home as a nice , smooth sphere . But mapping the Earth 's gravitational field provides a different view of the planet . <p> The geoid is an equipotential surface that can be thought of as the shape an ocean surface would take due to the Earth 's gravity field.VISUALIZATION COURTESY OF NASA <p> a new visualization of Earth looks nothing like the Blue Marble seen from space . <p> NASA has released a new geoid model showing the shape of Earth 's gravitational field . The slight , irregular bulges and depressions are caused by variations in the distribution of mass within the planet . It can also be imagined as the surface a global ocean would take if it were determined solely by Earth 's own gravity and rotation . <p> The visualization is an exaggerated geoid , with heights multiplied by a factor of 10,000 in order to show the variations in the gravitational field . NASA created this lumpy version of Earth using models and data @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at different locations . The dataset stretches back 15 years and includes a billion observations . NASA also shared an interactive 3D model of the geoid that you can explore here , as well as a longer video . <p> Measuring gravity has value beyond creating jarring visuals that 'll make you question just how round Earth is . NASA and the European Space Agency both have satellites that keep tabs on the planet 's gravitational field . <p> These observations have been used to get a better handle on how much ice Antarctica and Greenland are losing as the planet warms . NASA 's satellites -- which operate as part of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment ( GRACE ) -- show that Antarctica has lost approximately 135 gigatons of ice per year between 2002 and 2025 , while Greenland has lost 264 gigatons of ice annually over that same period . Improving those estimates is key to understanding how much oceans are rising now -- and how much more they 'll rise in the future . <p> The GRACE observations have also been used to track groundwater loss @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ groundwater depletion in the western US and elsewhere . It also provides information on more acute droughts : The extreme dryness that 's fueling fires in Spain and France this summer is visible in GRACE 's data . An analysis from the University of Nebraska using gravitational observations shows that soil moisture and shallow groundwater are both sitting in or near record-low territory in parts of the region . <p> With climate change set to make drought worse in many locations , these types of observations can provide valuable information to water managers in parched regions . <p> This story originally appeared onWIRED en Espa ? oland has been translated from Spanish . <p> Javier Carbajal is a contributor to WIRED en Espa ? ol .
